title: Dual Immunotherapy May Improve Early-Stage Breast Cancer Treatment
originalTitle: Cemiplimab and Fianlimab With Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy in Early-Stage High-Risk ERBB2-Negative Breast Cancer: The I-SPY2 Randomized Clinical Trial.
imageSearchQuery: breast cancer immunotherapy treatment
imageAltText: Illustration showing breast cancer cells being targeted by immune checkpoint inhibitor drugs.
imageCaption: Dual immune checkpoint inhibitors combined with chemotherapy improve tumor response in early-stage ERBB2-negative breast cancer, as studied in this trial.
blurb: Researchers tested adding two immune drugs, cemiplimab and fianlimab, to standard chemotherapy in early-stage, high-risk breast cancer patients without ERBB2 overexpression. They found this combination nearly doubled the rate of complete tumor disappearance before surgery compared to chemotherapy alone. This effect was strongest in patients with an active immune environment in their tumors.

They found this combination nearly doubled the rate of complete tumor disappearance before surgery compared to chemotherapy alone. This effect was strongest in patients with an active immune environment in their tumors.
curiosityHook: Combining two immune checkpoint drugs with chemotherapy may better shrink early breast tumors before surgery.
summary: This study focused on improving treatment for early-stage, high-risk breast cancer patients who do not have ERBB2-positive tumors. It was a randomized clinical trial called I-SPY2 conducted in multiple US medical centers. Researchers enrolled patients with early breast cancer and added two immune checkpoint blockers, cemiplimab (anti-PD-1) and fianlimab (anti-LAG-3), to the usual chemotherapy before surgery. The trial compared this combination to data from similar patients treated with chemotherapy alone. They measured pathologic complete response, meaning no detectable cancer remained at surgery. Adding both immune drugs improved this response rate from about 21% to 44% overall. The benefit was especially notable in triple-negative breast cancer and in patients whose tumors showed signs of immune activity. Some immune-related side effects occurred, like adrenal insufficiency. These results suggest combining these two checkpoint inhibitors with chemotherapy could improve tumor eradication before surgery in certain breast cancers. More trials are needed to confirm safety and long-term outcomes.
researchQuestion: Can combining two immune checkpoint inhibitors, cemiplimab and fianlimab, with standard chemotherapy improve tumor clearance before surgery in early-stage, high-risk ERBB2-negative breast cancer?
whatTheyDid: The researchers ran a randomized clinical trial called I-SPY2 involving patients with stage II or III ERBB2-negative breast cancer considered high risk. They enrolled 78 patients who received weekly paclitaxel chemotherapy for 12 weeks followed by doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide, then surgery. Along with paclitaxel, this group also received four doses of two immune checkpoint inhibitors, cemiplimab and fianlimab, every three weeks. Their outcomes were compared against a historical control group of 350 similar patients who received chemotherapy alone. The main result measured was pathologic complete response, indicating no visible tumor remaining during surgery. Biomarkers related to immune activity in tumors were also studied to see if they predicted treatment success.
whatTheyFound: The combination of cemiplimab and fianlimab with chemotherapy nearly doubled the complete tumor response rate from 21% in controls to 44% in treated patients. In triple-negative breast cancer, response increased from 29% to 53%, and in hormone receptor-positive, ERBB2-negative breast cancer, response improved from 14% to 36%. Patients with positive immune signatures in their tumors showed especially strong benefits. However, immune-related side effects like adrenal gland dysfunction occurred in about one-fifth of treated patients, with some experiencing serious inflammation of the pituitary gland. This indicates the treatment boosts the immune system’s ability to fight cancer but also increases risk of immune side effects.
mainResult: Adding both cemiplimab and fianlimab to chemotherapy improved tumor clearance before surgery in early-stage ERBB2-negative breast cancer.
whatThisCouldLeadTo: If further studies confirm these results, combining two immune checkpoint inhibitors with chemotherapy might become a more effective neoadjuvant (pre-surgery) treatment for high-risk breast cancer lacking ERBB2 overexpression. This could increase the chance that surgeries remove no active tumor, potentially improving long-term outcomes and survival in these patients. Doctors might tailor treatment based on tumor immune activity biomarkers to identify who would benefit most. Still, managing immune-related side effects will be crucial. Ongoing research and larger trials are needed to understand long-term safety, optimal dosing, and if this approach improves patient survival or reduces cancer recurrence.
deepDive: Breast cancer treatment often includes chemotherapy before surgery to shrink tumors and improve outcomes. However, some aggressive types, especially those that do not overexpress ERBB2, respond less well to standard chemotherapy alone. Immune checkpoint inhibitors are drugs that block proteins cancer cells use to hide from the immune system, allowing immune cells to attack tumors. Cemiplimab blocks PD-1, and fianlimab blocks LAG-3; both are checkpoint inhibitors but target different proteins that suppress immune responses. Combining two checkpoint blockers may enhance immune activation more than one alone. In this study, adding both drugs to chemotherapy aimed to boost the patient’s immune system to better fight the tumor. The researchers measured pathologic complete response, a strong indication that the tumor was eradicated by treatment before surgery. They also looked at immune-related biomarkers to see which tumors were more responsive. The combination nearly doubled response rates, especially in tumors with active immune signatures, supporting that the dual blockade helped the immune system overcome tumor defenses. However, stronger immune activation also caused some patients to develop adrenal gland problems, showing that the treatment can provoke serious immune side effects. This balance between stronger cancer-fighting and side effects is a key challenge for these therapies.

title: Brain Hub in Rats May Link Movement and Mood Disorders
originalTitle: Beyond the role in motor function, entopeduncular nucleus, a critical neural hub in psychiatric disorders and sleep regulation.
imageSearchQuery: entopeduncular nucleus brain anatomy
imageAltText: Diagram of rodent brain highlighting the entopeduncular nucleus as a small region deep in the basal ganglia
imageCaption: The entopeduncular nucleus (highlighted) is a key brain hub integrating movement and mood signals in rodents, studied to understand human brain disorders.
blurb: Researchers reviewed studies on the entopeduncular nucleus (EP), a brain region in rats similar to a part of the human brain. They found that the EP controls not only movement but also mood, addiction, anxiety, and sleep. This suggests the EP could be a target for treating psychiatric and motor disorders.
excerpt: Researchers reviewed studies on the entopeduncular nucleus (EP), a brain region in rats similar to a part of the human brain. curiosityHook: Did you know a single brain region helps control both movement and mood?
summary: This review focuses on the entopeduncular nucleus (EP), a key brain area in rats that corresponds to a human brain structure involved in motor and psychiatric functions. The authors gathered evidence from various rodent studies using methods like optogenetics, brain recordings, and behavior tests, plus human studies such as brain imaging and deep brain stimulation. They found that the EP processes many chemical signals and connects to other brain parts to regulate movement, mood, anxiety, addiction, and sleep. Disturbances in EP circuits are linked to diseases like depression, anxiety, and Parkinson's. By understanding how EP circuits work, scientists see potential for new therapies targeting these brain circuits. However, more research is needed to confirm these roles and develop treatments for humans.
researchQuestion: What roles does the entopeduncular nucleus play beyond motor control, especially in psychiatric and sleep-related functions?
whatTheyDid: The researchers conducted a narrative review, collecting and analyzing published experimental and clinical studies on the EP. They included findings from rodent studies using techniques like optogenetics to manipulate nerves, electrophysiology to measure brain activity, neuroanatomical tracing to map connections, and behavioral testing to assess emotions and actions. They also reviewed human studies involving brain imaging, lesion analysis, and deep brain stimulation focused on the EP or its human equivalent.
whatTheyFound: They found that the EP acts as a hub processing various chemical messages, including GABA, glutamate, dopamine, serotonin, and cannabinoids. The EP connects to the lateral habenula, which is involved in processing negative experiences, addiction, and mood. Specific EP circuits influence anxiety regulation. Problems with EP activity relate to depression, anxiety, and movement issues seen in Parkinson’s disease. Human and animal studies suggest that targeting EP circuits with brain stimulation could have therapeutic effects.
mainResult: The entopeduncular nucleus integrates motor and emotional signals and is linked to mood, addiction, sleep, and movement disorders.
whatThisCouldLeadTo: If future research confirms these findings, therapies targeting the EP could help treat mental health conditions like depression and anxiety, sleep problems, and motor disorders such as Parkinson’s disease. Brain stimulation or drugs aimed at EP circuits might become new treatments. This might also improve understanding of how brain hubs control both movement and mood, allowing better diagnostic tools or personalized interventions. While promising, such therapies require more studies and testing in humans before being considered safe or effective.
deepDive: The entopeduncular nucleus (EP) is part of the basal ganglia, a deep brain system controlling movement and emotion. In rodents, it matches the human internal globus pallidus, making it a valuable model for understanding human brain function. The EP receives and sends signals using multiple neurotransmitters, including inhibitory GABA and excitatory glutamate, as well as modulators like dopamine and serotonin. It sends major output signals to the lateral habenula, a brain area that detects negative events and influences mood and addiction behaviors. Researchers have used methods like optogenetics, which enables control of selected nerve cells with light, and chemogenetics, manipulating nerves with chemicals, to pinpoint how different EP circuits affect behaviors like anxiety or reward-seeking. Electrophysiological recordings track brain activity patterns in the EP during these behaviors. These approaches show that the EP is not just about moving the body but also about shaping emotional and psychiatric states. Dysfunction in these circuits might explain symptoms in depression, anxiety, and Parkinsonian motor problems. Understanding EP connectivity and signaling could open doors for targeted neuromodulation therapies that adjust brain activity in these circuits to restore healthier function.

Also, therapeutic approaches like brain stimulation targeting EP circuits are experimental and not proven effective or safe in patients. title: Review Finds Injury Studies Miss Indigenous Perspectives
originalTitle: Equity, evidence and indigenous knowledges in PROMs in Australian injury research: a systematic review.
imageSearchQuery: Australian Indigenous health injury recovery patient-reported measures
imageAltText: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples community health discussion
imageCaption: The study reviewed how Australian injury research includes Indigenous peoples’ perspectives in recovery measurement.
blurb: Researchers reviewed 11 Australian trauma studies using patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs). They found these tools rarely include Indigenous knowledge or consider health equity for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Priority groups like Indigenous communities and people with disabilities were often underrepresented or excluded.
excerpt: Researchers reviewed 11 Australian trauma studies using patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs). They found these tools rarely include Indigenous knowledge or consider health equity for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Priority groups like Indigenous communities and people with disabilities were often underrepresented or excluded.
curiosityHook: How well do injury studies reflect the voices and experiences of Indigenous Australians?
summary: This study focused on how Australian injury research uses patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) to assess recovery. The researchers performed a systematic review of 11 studies that measured trauma impacts on adults in Australia. They checked whether these studies included Indigenous peoples’ perspectives and considered health equity. The review found 17 different PROMs used, mostly assessing physical and mental health. However, none fully met criteria for equity-sensitive reporting or included Indigenous knowledges. Priority populations, such as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, culturally diverse groups, and people with disabilities, were frequently underrepresented or left out. This gap could limit understanding of recovery experiences for these groups. The authors highlight the urgent need to develop culturally safe and inclusive PROMs that reflect diverse recovery experiences. These improvements could better support equitable trauma care and follow-up for all Australians, especially Indigenous peoples. However, current findings are limited by the small number of studies and focus only on observational trauma research.
researchQuestion: Do Australian trauma studies use patient-reported outcome measures that include Indigenous perspectives and health equity?
whatTheyDid: The researchers systematically reviewed 11 observational Australian trauma studies focused on adults with injuries. They looked for studies that used patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) to assess health outcomes after injury. They extracted information on which PROMs were used and applied the CREATE and PROGRESS-PLUS tools to evaluate if Indigenous peoples were included and whether the studies addressed health equity-related factors. They checked how often priority populations like Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, culturally and linguistically diverse groups, people with disabilities, and women were represented. Their method carefully assessed both the presence of Indigenous knowledge and equity indicators in injury recovery measurement tools.
whatTheyFound: The review found 17 different PROMs used across the 11 studies. The most common PROMs focused on general physical and mental health outcomes, which were often shown to be impaired after injury with lasting effects. However, none of the studies fully addressed health equity criteria, and Indigenous knowledge was not incorporated into the PROMs. Priority groups including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, culturally diverse communities, people with disabilities, and women were frequently missing or underrepresented in these studies. This indicates significant gaps in how well injury recovery is measured in diverse Australian populations, limiting insights into the varied recovery experiences that exist especially for Indigenous people.
mainResult: Australian injury studies rarely include Indigenous perspectives or health equity in patient-reported outcome measures.
whatThisCouldLeadTo: If researchers develop PROMs that include Indigenous knowledge and explicitly address health equity, future injury studies could better capture the true recovery experiences of diverse Australian populations. This would help tailor trauma care and follow-up to meet the needs of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples as well as other priority groups often left out. More inclusive PROMs could guide policies and practices to reduce health disparities after injury. However, creating culturally safe and meaningful tools will require collaboration with Indigenous communities and careful validation. The improved understanding could support more equitable health outcomes and inform services that reflect patients' lived experiences across Australia.
deepDive: Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) are questionnaires that patients complete to report on their health, function, and quality of life after medical events like injury. PROMs provide valuable insights into recovery that clinical tests might miss. However, PROMs can only improve care if they reflect all patients’ experiences, including cultural values and unique health determinants. In Australia, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples face a higher burden of injury, yet their knowledge and perspectives are rarely included when measuring outcomes. This review analyzed Australian trauma studies for inclusion of Indigenous knowledge and health equity factors using validated appraisal tools. The analysis showed PROMs commonly used focus on general health domains but omit cultural safety and equity considerations. Priority groups were often underrepresented or excluded, which may skew understanding and conceal barriers to recovery unique to these populations. The research highlights the need to develop PROMs that are culturally adapted or co-designed with Indigenous communities, capturing their lived realities and determinants of health. This approach would generate more accurate, relevant data that can inform trauma care and rehabilitation programs designed to support diverse recovery needs. The absence of this currently limits efforts toward equitable health outcomes after injury in Australia.

title: Pathogens in Traditional Food Markets Could Threaten Health Globally
originalTitle: Market-source pathogens in traditional food markets, 2000-25: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
imageSearchQuery: traditional wet food market fish raw meat hygiene
imageAltText: A busy traditional food market with fresh fish, meat, and vegetables displayed in open stalls.
imageCaption: Traditional food markets often sell raw animal products that this study found to carry pathogens posing health risks.
blurb: Researchers studied contamination levels in traditional food markets worldwide by reviewing 247 studies from 41 countries. They found that about 15% of samples from these markets carried harmful bacteria, viruses, or parasites, with fish and seafood markets showing the highest contamination rates. This highlights key points where public health efforts could reduce disease risks from market-sourced foods.
excerpt: Researchers studied contamination levels in traditional food markets worldwide by reviewing 247 studies from 41 countries. They found that about 15% of samples from these markets carried harmful bacteria, viruses, or parasites, with fish and seafood markets showing the highest contamination rates. curiosityHook: Ever wonder how safe the food is at wet markets around the world? This study reveals surprising risks people might face.
summary: This study aimed to understand how common disease-causing microbes are in traditional food markets, often called wet markets, especially in low- and middle-income countries. The researchers conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of 247 studies published between 2000 and 2025. These studies tested for bacteria, viruses, and parasites in foods and surfaces from markets in 41 countries. They found that overall, about 15% of market samples were contaminated. Bacteria were the most common pathogens, followed by parasites and viruses. Markets selling fish and seafood had the highest contamination levels. Contamination was more common in raw animal products and environmental samples than in cooked foods or fruits and vegetables. The study found contamination levels did not significantly change over time. Higher quality studies tended to report lower contamination. This suggests that traditional markets remain hotspots for pathogens that can spread diseases to humans. The researchers highlight crucial points in the food chain where interventions could reduce risks. They recommend coordinated surveillance and more uniform future studies to better manage these health threats. However, the findings mainly combine existing studies and do not prove direct disease transmission from markets to people yet.
researchQuestion: How common are disease-causing bacteria, viruses, and parasites in foods and environments of traditional food markets worldwide? Which markets and food types pose higher risks?
whatTheyDid: The researchers collected data from studies published between 2000 and 2025 that reported detecting pathogens in traditional food markets. They included 247 studies covering 597 pathogen-sample combinations from 41 countries. They excluded studies with fewer than 20 samples, those not done in traditional markets, or lacking relevant data. The team analyzed the prevalence of pathogens in different market types and sample types, such as raw meat, fish, cooked foods, fruits, and environmental surfaces. They used statistical methods to calculate overall and subgroup contamination rates, study quality effects, and how prevalence changed over time.
whatTheyFound: The global pooled prevalence of pathogens in traditional food markets was about 15%. Bacteria were detected in 19% of samples, parasites in 27%, and viruses in 8%. Fish and seafood markets had the highest contamination rate at nearly 38%. Raw meat and environmental samples also showed high contamination, while cooked foods, fruits, vegetables, and worker samples had lower rates. The results suggest contamination generally decreases along the chain from animals and environment to ready-to-eat foods and humans. There was no clear change in contamination levels over time. Higher-quality studies reported lower contamination, hinting at potential measurement biases or improvements in some areas. These findings indicate traditional markets remain sources of pathogens that could cause infections in humans.
mainResult: About 15% of samples from traditional food markets worldwide carry bacteria, viruses, or parasites, especially in fish and seafood markets.
whatThisCouldLeadTo: If future research confirms how pathogens spread in these markets, efforts can focus on reducing contamination at key points, such as during fish and seafood handling. Better hygiene and targeted surveillance could lower disease risks for market workers and shoppers. This knowledge can help design health policies to make traditional markets safer, especially in low-income regions where they are critical food sources. More standardized and prospective studies could track effectiveness of improved practices. Eventually, these measures might reduce outbreaks of diseases linked to market foods without disrupting local access to fresh produce and animal products.
deepDive: Traditional food markets, including wet markets and live poultry markets, are common in many parts of the world and provide fresh food to millions, especially in low- and middle-income countries. However, these markets bring together live animals, food, humans, and the environment closely, creating opportunities for pathogens (like bacteria, viruses, and parasites) to spread. This study combined results from hundreds of previous research papers that tested for pathogens in market foods and surroundings. The researchers used meta-analysis, a statistical method that pools data from multiple studies, to estimate how widespread these pathogens are. They found that contamination is most common in raw animal products and seafood, which can harbor bacteria and parasites more easily. The lower contamination in cooked and plant-based foods reflects how food processing and cooking reduce pathogens. The presence of pathogens in environmental samples also points to hygiene challenges in market settings. There is a clear gradient showing how contamination decreases as food moves from animals to humans ready to eat. The study emphasizes that while these markets remain important for food access, they also present persistent risks which could be reduced through better practices and monitoring. However, the study does not directly link contamination with disease outbreaks in people, nor does it assess specific interventions yet. It mainly highlights where risks are highest for future cost-effective health measures.

title: Hybrid AI and Physics Models Could Improve Air Pollution Forecasts

curiosityHook: Can blending AI with physics make pollution forecasts clearer and more useful for everyone?
summary: This paper examines air pollution forecasting methods, focusing on physical models, statistical approaches, machine learning (ML), and hybrids. It is a review article that summarizes recent progress and emerging trends in air quality prediction. The authors looked at studies involving different forecasting techniques, highlighting new developments such as physics-informed ML and integrated systems. The paper points out key challenges like applying models in regions lacking data, measuring uncertainty, and making AI models understandable. It emphasizes the benefits of hybrid systems that merge physical science knowledge with AI strengths. Although these hybrid systems show promise, the paper notes that more work is needed to address uncertainty, operational issues, and public health integration. This study suggests future air pollution forecasting should combine accuracy with explainability and health impact awareness. However, current solutions are still developing and not yet fully operational worldwide.
researchQuestion: How do different methods—physical, statistical, and machine learning—compare and combine to forecast air pollution effectively? What are the challenges and promising directions in using hybrid models?
whatTheyDid: The researchers conducted a comprehensive review of recent literature covering various air pollution forecasting methods. They analyzed deterministic physical models, statistical forecasting techniques, machine learning approaches, and hybrid systems that combine these methods. They examined recent advancements like physics-informed machine learning, adaptive mesh refinement, and AI-assisted chemical transport models. They also assessed operational challenges including model transferability to regions with limited data, uncertainty quantification, interpretability of deep learning models, system robustness, and data quality issues. By summarizing and critiquing these developments, they identified gaps and future directions for air quality modeling.
whatTheyFound: Their review revealed that hybrid forecasting systems, which integrate physical models with machine learning, show the most promise for accurate and interpretable air pollution predictions. researchQuestion: Can an effective method be developed to genetically transform and perform CRISPR gene editing in Oxalis vulcanicola plants?
whatTheyDid: The researchers used stem segments from the Oxalis vulcanicola 'Sunset Velvet' plant as starting material. They measured how well the introduced gene was expressed using a marker enzyme (GUS). After finding optimal conditions, they produced eight stable genetically modified plants. Then, they applied the CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing technique to target the OvPDS1 gene, which affects pigment production, to create mutations and observe resulting changes in the plants.

mainResult: An effective method to genetically transform Oxalis plants and perform the first successful CRISPR editing in this species was established.
whatThisCouldLeadTo: This method could help scientists study gene functions in Oxalis and other ornamental plants that lacked genetic tools before. Researchers might also use this platform to explore genetic pathways important for plant health or flower quality. deepDive: Oxalis vulcanicola 'Sunset Velvet' is a popular ornamental plant, but studying its genetics was difficult because there was no reliable way to add or edit genes in it. Researchers tackled this by developing a transformation method using Agrobacterium tumefaciens, a bacterium known for naturally transferring DNA to plants. They used stem segments as starting material, as these can regenerate whole plants. By carefully optimizing infection conditions—like how long plant tissue was exposed to bacteria, how dense the bacterial cells were, and chemical additives (such as acetosyringone, which boosts bacterial DNA transfer)—they improved DNA insertion efficiency. They confirmed gene insertion by detecting a marker enzyme and regenerating stable modified plants. Next, they applied CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing technology, which uses a guide RNA to direct a DNA-cutting enzyme to a specific gene—in this case, the OvPDS1 gene, important for carotenoid pigments responsible for leaf coloration. DNA sequencing confirmed mutations at the target site, but this occurred in only a small fraction of plants, indicating the editing process still needs enhancement. This combined system of transformation and gene editing forms a basic genetic toolbox for Oxalis plants, making it possible to investigate gene roles and breed new variants. The low editing frequency is common in early gene editing attempts and suggests more work to optimize delivery, editing components, or tissue culture conditions is needed. Still, this study overcomes a major roadblock in functional genomics and breeding for a non-model ornamental species.

summary: This study focused on understanding why some older adults maintain strong cognitive abilities despite brain aging. Personalized medicine that tailors therapy based on molecular characteristics of each tumor is a promising direction to improve outcomes.

blurb: Researchers tested a combination of copanlisib, a PIK3CA inhibitor, with nivolumab, an immune therapy, on patients with advanced microsatellite stable colorectal cancer. curiosityHook: Can blocking a specific cancer mutation improve immune therapy success in tough colorectal cancers?
summary: This study focused on metastatic microsatellite stable colorectal cancer, which rarely responds well to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Researchers conducted a phase 1/2 clinical trial combining copanlisib, a drug that blocks PIK3CA mutations found in some colorectal cancers, with nivolumab, an immune-boosting antibody. They enrolled two patient groups: those with mutated PIK3CA and those without. The trial tested safety and effectiveness over six months. While the combination was well tolerated by patients, the number of tumor responses was very low, with only 2 out of 22 mutation-positive patients showing improvement. Survival times and disease control rates did not significantly differ between groups. The findings suggest that this drug combo may not strongly help most patients with this cancer type. More research is needed to find better therapies or understand which patients might benefit.
researchQuestion: Does combining copanlisib and nivolumab improve treatment outcomes for patients with metastatic microsatellite stable colorectal cancer, especially those with PIK3CA mutations?
whatTheyDid: The researchers conducted a clinical trial involving two groups of patients with advanced microsatellite stable colorectal cancer. One group had tumors with PIK3CA mutations, and the other did not. Patients received combination therapy: copanlisib, a PIK3CA inhibitor given at 60 mg on days 1, 8, and 15 of a 28-day cycle, plus nivolumab, an anti-PD-1 immune therapy given at 480 mg on day one. The trial monitored safety, tumor response rates at 6 months, progression-free survival, overall survival, and disease control rates.
whatTheyFound: The combination treatment was generally well tolerated with manageable side effects. However, in the group without PIK3CA mutations, none of the 17 patients showed an objective tumor response at 6 months. In the mutation-positive group, only 2 of 22 patients responded. Median progression-free survival was about 1.6 to 1.7 months, and overall survival ranged from 6.7 to 8.5 months, with no meaningful difference between groups. The duration of response, when present, was over a year. Disease control rates at 6 months were low and did not differ significantly. Overall, the drug combo demonstrated limited effectiveness against this form of colorectal cancer.
mainResult: Combining copanlisib with nivolumab is safe but shows limited tumor response in advanced microsatellite stable colorectal cancer patients, regardless of PIK3CA mutation status.
whatThisCouldLeadTo: If future studies identify patient subgroups more likely to respond or optimize dosing schedules, this combination might become a treatment option for some colorectal cancer patients resistant to current therapies. Additionally, understanding why most patients do not benefit could guide development of more effective drug combinations or novel agents. The trial also helps establish safe dosing for further research. Since immune therapies alone often fail in microsatellite stable colorectal cancer, combining them with targeted inhibitors remains an area of interest but needs more work to improve outcomes.
deepDive: Colorectal cancer with microsatellite stability tends to resist immune treatments because the tumors produce few signals to attract immune cells. The PIK3CA gene mutation, present in about 15% of colorectal cancers, can affect cell growth and immune responses. Copanlisib inhibits proteins made by mutated PIK3CA, possibly reducing tumor growth and changing the immune environment. Nivolumab blocks PD-1, a protein that cancer uses to hide from immune cells, potentially restoring immune attack. By combining these drugs, researchers hoped copanlisib might make the tumor more visible to immune cells, boosting nivolumab’s effect. In this phase 1/2 trial, the combo was tested for safety and early effectiveness. Although it was safe, objective responses were rare, suggesting that PI3K inhibition alone may not sufficiently change the tumor environment to enhance immune attack in these patients. The study measured progression-free survival (time without tumor growth), overall survival, and disease control to understand treatment impact. While some patients had longer responses, most saw limited benefit. This indicates a complex tumor biology that resists current strategies, highlighting the need for more targeted or combination approaches to overcome resistance.

curiosityHook: Could turning food scraps into compost both fight pollution and quietly add plastic to soil?
summary: This study examined if recycling food waste in the US by composting and anaerobic digestion reduces environmental problems. The researchers used mass balance modeling and life cycle assessment to compare the current practice, mostly landfilling food waste, with hypothetical nationwide recycling. They analyzed impacts on climate change, nutrient runoff into waterways, and plastic contamination in soils. However, applying compost and digestate to fields would only slightly replace synthetic fertilizers, less than 2%. More work is needed to design better food packaging to avoid plastic buildup in farming soils while advancing recycling.
researchQuestion: How does recycling food waste in the US by composting and anaerobic digestion compare to landfilling in terms of climate impact, nutrient pollution, and soil plastic contamination?
whatTheyDid: The researchers built a mass balance model and performed life cycle assessment to analyze the environmental outcomes of different food waste management methods across the US. They compared the current dominant practice of landfilling food waste with scenarios where food scraps are recycled through composting and anaerobic digestion. The model estimated greenhouse gas emissions, nutrient runoff (nitrogen and phosphorus) into waterways, and the amount of plastic pollution transferred to soils from compost and digestate application. They evaluated national scale impacts to get overall estimates rather than localized results. This approach allowed detailed comparison of emissions, nutrient flows, and plastic contaminant spread under varying waste management strategies.
whatTheyFound: The study found that shifting from landfilling to organics recycling could cut greenhouse gas emissions from US food waste by 89 to 99%. It could also reduce nitrogen and phosphorus loading into downstream waterways by roughly 49-54% and 78-98%, respectively. Despite these reductions, the fertilizers supplied by compost and digestate from recycled food waste would only replace less than 2% of US mineral nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizer use annually. Importantly, the team identified a trade-off: without novel packaging solutions, recycling food waste could introduce about 20,000 tons of plastic particles every year into US agricultural soils through compost and digestate application. This highlights an unintended environmental risk alongside the benefits.
mainResult: Recycling US food waste massively lowers emissions and nutrient pollution but risks adding significant plastic to soils.
whatThisCouldLeadTo: If food waste recycling is widely adopted, the US could dramatically cut damaging greenhouse gases and nutrient pollution affecting water quality. This would help combat climate change and protect aquatic ecosystems. However, the identified accumulation of plastic in farm soils could harm soil health and crop growth over time unless packaging materials improve. Future research and innovation are needed to design food packaging that biodegrades safely or avoids plastics to prevent soil contamination. Governments and industry might also develop guidelines or policies to control plastic inputs via recycling. Overall, the study guides efforts to maximize environmental benefits from food waste recycling while minimizing hidden plastic pollution risks.

This study used mass balance modeling to track the flow of nutrients and materials through these recycling processes on a national scale. This plastic pollution could harm soil organisms and reduce soil quality over time, potentially undermining agricultural sustainability. The study highlights the need to rethink packaging design and waste processing to fully realize environmental benefits from food waste recycling.

summary: Tissues in the body, such as bone, cartilage, and blood vessels, are not uniform; their properties change depending on direction, a feature called anisotropy. This characteristic is crucial for their strength and function. This paper is a comprehensive review that explores the natural causes of anisotropy in tissues, like how collagen fibers are arranged and how tissue structure varies across layers. The authors examined traditional scaffold-making methods, including freeze-casting, mechanical anchoring, and electrospinning, focusing on their ability to create anisotropic structures. They also reviewed new precise fabrication techniques, especially 3D printing, which offers better control over scaffold architecture. The paper discusses hybrid combining methods that may overcome limitations seen in conventional approaches. The authors provide a framework for designing future scaffolds that better replicate real tissue architectures, potentially improving their effectiveness. However, this work is a review and does not include new experiments, so practical outcomes of these advanced methods require further testing in labs and clinics.
researchQuestion: What methods best create scaffolds that imitate the directional structure (anisotropy) of native tissues such as bone, tendon, and cartilage?
whatTheyDid: The authors conducted a detailed review analyzing how native tissues achieve anisotropic properties through structures like collagen fiber orientation and hierarchical organization. They systematically compared various established scaffold fabrication methods, such as freeze-casting (which uses controlled freezing to create aligned pores), mechanical anchoring, and electrospinning (which produces aligned fibers). They then discussed recent advances in additive manufacturing (3D printing) techniques for creating scaffolds with precise, customizable anisotropy. Finally, they explored hybrid fabrication strategies that combine these methods to address limitations of individual approaches.
whatTheyFound: The review found that while traditional methods like freeze-casting and electrospinning can induce anisotropy, they face challenges with fine architectural control and scaling up production. Additive manufacturing advances offer improved precision and tunability, allowing creation of complex, tissue-like anisotropic scaffolds. Hybrid strategies that integrate multiple methods appear promising to better replicate natural tissue architectures. Overall, the paper highlights that reproducing the directional and hierarchical features of tissues remains a challenge but new fabrication techniques could bridge this gap.
mainResult: Advanced and hybrid fabrication methods could produce more precise, anisotropic scaffolds that better mimic native tissue structures.
whatThisCouldLeadTo: If fabrication methods continue improving, scientists could build scaffold materials that closely replicate the complex directional structures of natural tissues. This would allow for engineered scaffolds that better support cell growth and tissue repair in bone, tendon, cartilage, and blood vessels. Such improvements may enhance the effectiveness of tissue engineering treatments by creating grafts that behave more like real tissues under mechanical stress. These scaffolds might enable more successful healing after injury or disease by matching native tissue properties more closely. However, more experimental testing is needed to translate design principles into practical, implantable scaffolds.

This structural feature arises from how collagen fibers and other components are organized in layers and gradients. To create scaffolds that mimic this, scientists use various fabrication methods. Freeze-casting slowly freezes a slurry to produce aligned pores resembling tissue structure. Electrospinning produces thin fibers aligned in one direction, mimicking fibrous tissue. Mechanical anchoring applies tension to guide fiber orientation. These older methods can induce some anisotropy but lack exact control over complex architecture and can be hard to scale. New additive manufacturing, like 3D printing, allows building scaffolds layer by layer with precise geometry and tunable fiber orientation. Combining traditional and additive methods in hybrid approaches aims to capture the best of both worlds—complex, hierarchical anisotropy with better manufacturability. This review gathers and compares these methods to help design next-gen scaffolds that more closely replicate tissue structure-function relationships.

Additionally, the model uses a learned attention mechanism to weigh sequences by evolutionary importance, enabling discovery of subfamily-specific interaction contacts.

This mechanism helps the model spot where proteins bind in a complex. This makes the approach more accessible and computationally efficient for widespread use.

It enables studying multiple gene edits, like analyzing gene families, without extra marker cleanup. The approach was demonstrated successfully in Chlamydomonas with nitrate reductase and a test target gene, showing practical potential. Still, further work is needed to test scalability, efficiency in other genes or organisms, and long-term stability of edited strains.

summary: This study focused on improving how scientists measure metabolites of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in urine, which indicate exposure to harmful air pollutants. The researchers developed a new laboratory method that can detect 18 different VOC metabolites, even though these chemicals have very different properties. They prepared urine samples by adding special labeled standards, then used an extraction technique designed to separate acidic and basic compounds efficiently. The combined samples were analyzed by liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry in one run, detecting chemicals under opposite electrical charges for better accuracy. Their method showed very low detection limits and met strict quality controls, including external proficiency testing. They then applied this method to urine samples from the China National Human Biomonitoring Program and found significant differences in metabolite levels across diverse groups. researchQuestion: Can a single laboratory method simultaneously measure multiple classes of volatile organic compound metabolites in urine despite their different chemical properties?
whatTheyDid: The researchers designed a new analytical method to quantify 18 urinary metabolites from VOCs. They first added isotope-labeled internal standards to urine samples for accurate tracking. The samples were acidified and loaded onto special solid-phase extraction plates to separate acidic and basic metabolites based on their acid-base chemistry. The acidic compounds were collected in one fraction, while basic ones were caught in another, which was then alkalized and re-extracted. These fractions were recombined and analyzed in one liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry run using electrospray ionization in both negative and positive modes. They validated this method by testing detection limits, performing quality control with reference materials, and passing an external proficiency test. Finally, they measured VOC metabolite levels in human urine from a national biomonitoring program in China and compared concentrations across different population groups.
whatTheyFound: The method successfully detected 18 VOC metabolites ranging widely in chemical nature, including acidic mercapturic and carboxylic acids as well as basic pyrrolidine alkaloids. The test showed very low detection limits, from 0.01 to 2.77 micrograms per liter, indicating high sensitivity. Quality control samples matched certified ranges closely, and the approach passed an external quality assessment, confirming its reliability. Applying the method to real-world urine samples from the China National Human Biomonitoring Program revealed meaningful differences in VOC metabolite concentrations between various subgroups, such as age, gender, or exposure levels. This demonstrates the method's practical use for detailed population exposure studies.
mainResult: A single laboratory test can accurately measure 18 diverse urinary VOC metabolites simultaneously using a combined extraction and analysis process.
whatThisCouldLeadTo: If widely adopted, this method could help public health researchers monitor exposure to multiple harmful air pollutants efficiently and comprehensively through urine testing. Additionally, the technique’s high sensitivity may aid early detection of exposure before health problems develop. However, using the test to predict health outcomes or exposure sources will require further studies linking metabolite levels to effects and exposure details. Still, this method lays important groundwork for accessible and thorough chemical exposure biomonitoring.

whatTheyDid: The researchers conducted a matched case-control study across three cancer centers in India. They recruited women diagnosed with breast cancer and matched them by age to women without cancer as controls. Breast cancer cases were categorized into four molecular subtypes based on hormone receptor and HER2 receptor status. They then applied multivariable conditional logistic regression to assess which risk factors were specifically associated with each breast cancer subtype.
whatTheyFound: They found that the most common breast cancer subtype was HR+HER2-. whatTheyDid: The team worked with pregnant Merino sheep to model preterm birth conditions. They divided the sheep into three groups: one received a saline solution as a control, another got high-dose antenatal steroids known as betamethasone, and the third was exposed to infection by injecting bacterial lipopolysaccharide to cause chorioamnionitis. Treatments were given either 2 or 8 days before the lambs were delivered prematurely 16 days early. After birth, the female lambs' ovaries were collected and analyzed using RNA sequencing to study gene activity changes. The ovaries also underwent detailed tissue examinations to count different egg follicle stages and check for signs of cell death or changes in ovarian cell types.

Steroid exposure increased markers of apoptosis, indicating more programmed cell death in ovary tissues. Infection reduced the number of primary (early) follicles, which are crucial for future fertility, and tended to increase dying or abnormal follicles. No clear changes were found in the stromal cells or other ovary cell types. These findings suggest that prenatal steroid use and chorioamnionitis can cause acute molecular and structural damage to the developing ovary, which may impact the ovary’s reserve of eggs and reproductive lifespan.
mainResult: Antenatal steroids and chorioamnionitis cause harmful molecular and structural changes in fetal ovaries of preterm sheep.
whatThisCouldLeadTo: Understanding how steroids and infection affect ovary development could influence how doctors manage pregnancies at risk of preterm birth. If these findings apply to humans, they suggest that exposure to these factors before birth might reduce the number of viable eggs a female has, potentially leading to delayed puberty or an earlier menopause. This knowledge may guide future strategies to protect or monitor female reproductive health after early birth and help refine treatments given to pregnant mothers to minimize long-term reproductive effects on their children. The researchers compared clinical features and pregnancy outcomes with patients who did not have adenomyosis. They found that patients with certain adenomyosis types had larger uteruses and different coexisting conditions. The live birth rates did not differ significantly between subtypes or compared to patients without adenomyosis. However, those with adenomyosis had lower chances of embryo implantation. Some ultrasound measurements suggested that thinner zones in the uterus were linked to better birth outcomes, but thicker uterine lining might reduce implantation success. researchQuestion: Do different ultrasound-detected adenomyosis subtypes affect clinical characteristics and reproductive outcomes after first frozen embryo transfer with hormone pretreatment?
whatTheyDid: This retrospective cohort study involved 179 infertility patients with adenomyosis and 179 without. All adenomyosis patients received an ultralong treatment with gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists (GnRHa) before undergoing their first frozen embryo transfer (FET) cycle. Adenomyosis diagnosis and subtype classification used two- and three-dimensional transvaginal ultrasound, categorizing lesions by type (diffuse, focal, mixed) and position within the uterine muscle wall (inner or outer). The researchers collected data on patient histories, uterine ultrasound features, and pregnancy outcomes after the first FET. They analyzed implantation rates, clinical pregnancy rates, miscarriage rates, and live birth rates, comparing results across adenomyosis subtypes and to those without the condition.
whatTheyFound: Patients with internal adenomyosis had a higher frequency of secondary infertility, while external adenomyosis was more often linked to ovarian endometriosis. Those with diffuse and internal adenomyosis showed larger uteruses and thicker anterior uterine walls than those with focal or external adenomyosis. Importantly, live birth rates after first FET cycles were similar between all groups. However, adenomyosis patients had a significantly reduced embryo implantation rate compared to controls. Exploratory analysis indicated that a greater reduction in the junctional zone (a specific uterine muscle area) thickness after treatment was associated with higher chances of live birth. Conversely, increased thickness of the uterine lining (endometrium) was linked to implantation failures. Due to the study's retrospective design and small subgroup sizes, these associations should be interpreted cautiously.
mainResult: Adenomyosis subtypes show distinct clinical features and are linked to lower embryo implantation rates after frozen embryo transfer, though live birth rates remain similar.
whatThisCouldLeadTo: If future research confirms these findings, ultrasound-based adenomyosis subtyping could help doctors personalize fertility treatments. Understanding which adenomyosis types respond better to hormone pretreatment may optimize embryo implantation chances. This could guide doctors in selecting patients who might benefit from specific therapies or closer monitoring during frozen embryo transfer. Still, more studies are needed to verify how ultrasound features predict outcomes and to develop precise treatment plans tailored to adenomyosis subtype. This research moves toward more informed infertility treatment but does not yet change clinical practice.
